summary:
Sol Teris is an interactive moon exploration environment which allows its users to determine whether a given lander or rover will be able to see the Sun, maintain communication with Earth and move with limited battery energy. It was developed to participate in the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge which involves the use of data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter concerning the terrain of the Moon and computed positions of the Sun and Earth relative to it.

The user explores the three-dimensional model of the Moon, compares different mission sites and connects the points into the path of a rover. Basic information regarding visibility of the Sun, visibility of the Earth and an estimate of battery reach is provided by simple information cards. Range rings allow for adjusting the distance a rover will be able to travel in different directions with regard to its battery capacity and terrain slopes. Scientific and Education modes provide advanced and basic levels of analysis of the task respectively and also there is a playable rover mission.

Selecting a lunar landing site involves power management, communication and movement issues which Sol Teris visualizes effectively.
details:
Sol Teris is an interactive lunar landing-site navigator that helps users explore three connected questions: Will a site receive enough sunlight? Can it maintain direct contact with Earth? How far could a rover travel with its available battery?

Near the Moon’s south pole, the Sun stays low in the sky. A nearby ridge can block sunlight, while crater walls can interrupt the view of Earth. Sol Teris makes these relationships visible by combining NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) terrain measurements with calculated Sun and Earth positions.

How it works

For each site, the project traces the surrounding terrain skyline, accounting for the Moon’s curvature. It then checks whether the Sun and Earth clear that skyline. Precomputed visibility data supports comparisons across 2027–2029, while live calculations provide conditions at the selected time and refine sunrise, sunset, Earthrise, and Earthset estimates.

Users can explore a 3D Moon, compare sites and dates, examine shadows, and investigate how a delayed landing changes conditions. Scientific tools include mission power estimates, terrain-aware rover routing, a calculator, and first-order launch-window and flight-path estimates.

Education mode presents the same underlying science in simpler language. Its information cards emphasize sunlight visibility, Earth visibility, and estimated battery range. Users can select rover-path points and adjust available battery charge. Directional range rings show how terrain slopes and energy limits affect one-way reach. A playable rover mission reinforces the connection between sunlight, power, communication, and survival.

Benefits and intended impact

Sol Teris helps students, educators, space enthusiasts, and early-stage mission planners understand the tradeoffs behind lunar exploration. A site with frequent sunlight may still have communication blackouts; a destination that looks close may exceed a rover’s battery range. Presenting these conditions together encourages users to evaluate a mission as a connected system.

The project supports education and exploratory analysis. Its simplified engineering models are estimates, rather than flight-qualified mission predictions.

Tools and development

The application uses TypeScript, React, and Vite for its interface; Three.js and custom shaders for the 3D Moon; and astronomy-engine for celestial positions. Python and NumPy support terrain processing, while Web Workers handle demanding browser calculations. The application runs on ordinary computers without specialized hardware.

NASA terrain data provides the measured landscape, and NASA’s RASSOR model supports the rover experience. The astronomy calculations were checked against JPL Horizons. AI coding assistance was used during development and is documented in the repository.

Creativity and design considerations

The project connects a whole-Moon view with local terrain, visibility calculations, and an interactive rover experience. Users can see a shadow, understand what terrain causes it, and explore its consequences for power and communication.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, data resolution, accessibility, browser performance, and clarity. We distinguish measured terrain from optional procedural visual detail, and real astronomical conditions from illustrative game rules. Separate Education and Scientific modes make the project approachable while preserving access to the methods and assumptions behind the results.
